blocks.content: Picture sitting in a cafe on public WiFi, opening a website, and typing in a username and password. If that site uses plain HTTP, the data leaves your laptop like an open postcard, anyone positioned between you and the server, a hacker on the same WiFi, a compromised router, can read it in plain text. If the same site uses HTTPS, that same data is locked inside a sealed box before it ever leaves your machine, only the destination server holds the key to open it.

HTTP and HTTPS are both application layer protocols for transferring web data, and the entire difference between them comes down to one word, security. This topic covers exactly what that security consists of, TLS and certificates, how HTTP itself has evolved across several versions, the actual request and response structure both protocols share, and what really happens end to end the moment you open a secure website.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273497949-80556065.png
blocks.alt: The same data, sent as an open postcard anyone can read, or sealed inside a locked box only the destination can open

blocks.content: HTTPS is HTTP plus TLS, the S stands for Secure. The protocol itself does not change, you still send GET, POST, headers, and bodies. TLS is a security layer underneath that encrypts everything before it ever touches the wire.
1. The HTTP Problem: Plain Text on the Wire
blocks.text: 1. The HTTP Problem: Plain Text on the Wire

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273500029-882508634.png
blocks.alt: Anyone running a packet sniffer on the same network can read an HTTP password exactly as it was typed

blocks.content: HTTP sends requests and responses as readable text. Anyone positioned between you and the server, a router, an internet provider, a coffee shop WiFi operator, or a genuine attacker, can read every request and response passing through, including a password typed directly into a login form.

blocks.title: Why Browsers Warn You
blocks.content: This is exactly why modern browsers flag a plain HTTP site as Not Secure, it is telling you, plainly, that you are about to send a postcard instead of a locked box, for absolutely any information the page collects.
2. TLS: What Actually Makes HTTPS Secure
blocks.text: 2. TLS: What Actually Makes HTTPS Secure

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024510-942115313.png
blocks.alt: TLS sits directly between your application's HTTP traffic and the underlying TCP connection carrying it

blocks.content: TLS, Transport Layer Security, sits between HTTP and TCP. Before a single HTTP request is sent, TLS performs its own handshake to agree on encryption algorithms and exchange the keys both sides will use, covered in full detail in the dedicated TLS Handshake topic.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273503314-466021652.png
blocks.alt: TLS provides three distinct guarantees at once, not just encryption alone

blocks.content: TLS provides three separate guarantees. Encryption means the data is unreadable to anyone eavesdropping on the connection. Authentication means the server's certificate proves you are actually talking to the real server, not an impostor. Integrity means any tampering with the data in transit is detected immediately, rather than silently accepted.
3. Certificates and the Chain of Trust
blocks.text: 3. Certificates and the Chain of Trust

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024987-913672351.png
blocks.alt: A website's own certificate is vouched for by an intermediate authority, which is itself vouched for by a trusted root

blocks.content: A server's TLS certificate contains its public key and is signed by a Certificate Authority, a trusted third party. Your browser ships with a built in list of root authorities it already trusts, and when a server presents its certificate, the browser checks whether it was signed by someone in that trusted chain, whether the domain name actually matches, and whether the certificate has expired.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273506431-643419397.png
blocks.alt: A certificate itself carries the domain name, a public key, a validity window, and the issuing authority's own signature

blocks.content: ["The domain name the certificate is actually valid for","The server's public key, used during the TLS handshake","A validity period, a start date and an expiry date","The issuing Certificate Authority's own digital signature over all of it"]
items: The domain name the certificate is actually valid for
The server's public key, used during the TLS handshake
A validity period, a start date and an expiry date
The issuing Certificate Authority's own digital signature over all of it

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273507997-606173868.png
blocks.alt: A valid certificate proves domain ownership, it never proves the organization behind that domain is trustworthy

blocks.content: A certificate only proves the server genuinely owns the domain, not that the company behind it is legitimate. A convincingly named phishing domain can obtain a perfectly valid HTTPS certificate too. HTTPS means the connection itself is encrypted, it says nothing about whether you should trust the destination.

This is exactly why a browser's padlock icon should never be read as this website is safe, only as no one in between can read or tamper with this specific connection, verifying the destination itself deserves your trust is a genuinely separate judgment call the padlock has no opinion on at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025328-862554817.png
blocks.alt: A self-signed certificate skips the trusted authority entirely, which is why browsers refuse to trust it by default

blocks.content: A server can also generate and sign its own certificate rather than obtaining one from a Certificate Authority at all. This works perfectly well for encryption itself, but since no browser's trusted root list includes that server's own signature, every visitor sees a warning by default. This is common and acceptable for internal tools or local development environments, where the small set of people who need access can manually tell their own browser to trust that one specific certificate, but it is never appropriate for a public facing production site.
4. HTTP Versions: How the Protocol Evolved
blocks.text: 4. HTTP Versions: How the Protocol Evolved

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273511307-478798177.png
blocks.alt: Each new HTTP version solved a specific performance problem the previous one had

blocks.content: HTTP/1.0 opened a brand new TCP connection for every single request, so a page with many assets meant many separate handshakes, genuinely slow. HTTP/1.1 improved this by reusing one connection across many requests, but those requests still had to be handled one after another, each one waiting for the previous response before starting.

HTTP/2 introduced multiplexing, many requests and responses interleaved over the very same single TCP connection at once, removing that one-at-a-time restriction while still running on ordinary TCP. HTTP/3 goes a step further, built on QUIC over UDP instead of TCP, eliminating TCP's own head of line blocking entirely, covered in depth in the TCP vs UDP topic, where one lost packet no longer stalls every other in-flight request on the connection.

Every version past HTTP/1.0 still speaks the same request and response vocabulary, methods, status codes, headers, an HTTP/3 request looks identical to an HTTP/1.1 one at the application level, the difference is entirely in how efficiently that request actually travels underneath.

blocks.title: HTTP/2 Is, in Practice, HTTPS Only
blocks.content: Nothing in the HTTP/2 specification technically requires encryption, but every major browser only actually implements HTTP/2 over TLS, never over plain HTTP, which means adopting HTTP/2's real performance benefits in practice also means adopting HTTPS.
5. Request and Response Structure
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273513099-220210625.png
blocks.alt: Regardless of version, HTTP is always a request carrying a method, path, headers, and body, answered by a response carrying a status code, headers, and body

blocks.content: The core protocol, regardless of version, is request and response. A request carries a method, GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, a path, a set of headers, and an optional body. A response carries back a status code, its own headers, and an optional body.

6. HTTPS End to End: What Actually Happens
blocks.text: 6. HTTPS End to End: What Actually Happens

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024508-237452996.png
blocks.alt: Four distinct steps happen before your browser ever displays a single byte of the page you asked for

blocks.content: Opening a secure website triggers a specific sequence before any content appears. First, the browser performs DNS resolution to find the server's IP address, covered in the dedicated DNS topic. Next, a TCP connection is established through the three way handshake, covered in the OSI Model and TCP vs UDP topics. After that, the TLS handshake happens, the server presents its certificate, the browser verifies it, and both sides agree on encryption keys, the exact mechanics of that exchange are covered in full in the dedicated TLS Handshake topic. Only then does the browser send its actual HTTP request, already encrypted, and the server's response comes back encrypted too, decrypted only once it reaches your browser.

None of these four steps are visible to the person using the browser, all of it happens within a fraction of a second, and a page that feels instant to load has still genuinely completed a DNS lookup, a full network handshake, and a cryptographic key exchange before rendering a single pixel.
7. HTTP vs HTTPS at a Glance
blocks.text: 7. HTTP vs HTTPS at a Glance

blocks.content: {"headers":["Property","HTTP","HTTPS"],"rows":[["Data on the wire","Plain, readable text","Encrypted ciphertext"],["Server identity","Not verified at all","Verified through a certificate"],["Tampering detection","None","Any modification in transit is detected"],["Setup cost","None beyond the TCP handshake","An additional TLS handshake"],["Default port","80","443"],["Browser treatment","Flagged as Not Secure","Shown as a secure connection"]]}
8. Ports: 80 and 443
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273516343-465850152.png
blocks.alt: A URL with no port specified quietly assumes port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS

blocks.content: When a URL does not specify a port explicitly, the protocol itself decides which one is used. HTTP defaults to port 80, HTTPS defaults to port 443. This is why the exact same domain can serve a plain, unencrypted response on one port and a fully encrypted one on the other, and why a server correctly configured for HTTPS but still listening on port 80 needs its own explicit redirect to actually enforce security.

Port 443 also tends to stay open even on restrictive corporate or public networks that otherwise block most outbound traffic, since blocking the same port every secure website in the world depends on would break far too much legitimate use, which is part of why so many modern protocols, including QUIC and HTTP/3, are specifically designed to look like ordinary encrypted web traffic on that same familiar port.
9. HSTS: Forcing HTTPS Automatically
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273518001-9699990.png
blocks.alt: Once a browser sees an HSTS header, it refuses to ever try plain HTTP for that site again, even if a user explicitly types it

blocks.content: A simple redirect from HTTP to HTTPS still means the very first request briefly touches plain HTTP before being redirected, a small but genuine window of exposure. HTTP Strict Transport Security, HSTS, closes that gap. Once a browser has visited a site over HTTPS and received this header, it remembers for a set period and refuses to ever attempt a plain HTTP connection to that domain again, automatically upgrading any attempt, even one a user typed manually, before a single byte is sent.

blocks.title: HSTS Has a Real Trade-Off
blocks.content: Because the browser remembers this instruction for a set duration, misconfiguring HSTS on a domain that later needs to drop HTTPS temporarily can lock out visitors entirely until that remembered period expires, which is exactly why it is rolled out carefully, often with a short duration at first.

Some domains go a step further and submit themselves to a browser-maintained preload list, meaning even a brand new visitor who has never touched that domain before still never attempts a plain HTTP connection to it even once, closing the small gap HSTS alone still leaves on a genuinely first-ever visit.
10. The Performance Cost of TLS, and How It Shrank
blocks.text: 10. The Performance Cost of TLS, and How It Shrank

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273519701-166620061.png
blocks.alt: Newer TLS versions and session resumption both exist specifically to shrink the extra round trips HTTPS costs over plain HTTP

blocks.content: Encryption is not free, the TLS handshake itself costs additional round trips beyond TCP's own three way handshake, extra latency an unencrypted HTTP connection never pays at all. TLS 1.3 cut this cost significantly compared to TLS 1.2, reducing the handshake to a single round trip in the common case, and session resumption goes even further, letting a returning visitor skip almost the entire handshake by reusing security parameters agreed on during an earlier visit.

This is exactly why the initial idea that HTTPS is meaningfully slower than HTTP has become far less true in practice, modern TLS combined with HTTP/2's multiplexing and session resumption together close most of the performance gap that once made teams hesitate to encrypt everything by default.

For most ordinary web traffic today, the honest answer to does HTTPS slow my site down is no, not meaningfully, and the remaining cost is small enough that it is rarely a legitimate reason to leave any part of a real production system on plain HTTP.
11. A Common Mistake: Mixed Content
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024987-490582472.png
blocks.alt: A single resource loaded over plain HTTP on an otherwise secure page quietly reopens the exact risk HTTPS exists to close

blocks.content: A page served correctly over HTTPS that still loads even one image, script, or stylesheet over plain HTTP creates a mixed content problem, that one resource travels completely unencrypted, readable and modifiable by anyone in between, even though the rest of the page looks perfectly secure in the browser's address bar. Modern browsers block or flag this specifically because it quietly undermines the entire point of serving the page securely in the first place.

An actively malicious version of this same gap is worse still, an attacker capable of intercepting that one plain HTTP request can modify it in transit, for instance silently swapping in a different script than the one the page actually intended to load, entirely defeating the protection the rest of the page's HTTPS was supposed to provide.
12. A Common Mistake: Ignoring Certificate Expiry
blocks.text: 12. A Common Mistake: Ignoring Certificate Expiry

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273533549-247204228.png
blocks.alt: An expired certificate greets every single visitor with a security warning, regardless of how well the rest of the system is running

blocks.content: A certificate that is not renewed before its expiry date causes every visitor to see a browser security warning the instant it lapses, even if every other part of the system is healthy and running perfectly. This is why production systems automate certificate renewal well ahead of the expiry date rather than relying on a person remembering a calendar reminder.

blocks.title: Automate This Specifically
blocks.content: Certificate expiry is one of the most common, entirely preventable causes of a sudden, embarrassing outage, since nothing about the server or application actually broke, only a date passed unnoticed.
13. Security Headers Beyond HSTS
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273535532-241202153.png
blocks.alt: HTTPS itself only secures the connection, these headers close off entirely different classes of attack on top of it

blocks.content: HTTPS secures the connection itself, but a handful of additional response headers close off other real attack surfaces entirely independent of encryption. Content Security Policy restricts which scripts are allowed to run on a page at all, meaningfully limiting the damage a successful script injection could otherwise do. X-Frame-Options blocks the page from being silently embedded inside another site's frame, a technique used in clickjacking attacks. X-Content-Type-Options stops the browser from guessing a file's type based on its content rather than trusting the server's declared type, closing off a specific class of file upload attack.

None of these headers require TLS to function technically, but they are almost always deployed together with HTTPS in practice, since a team investing in encrypting the connection is, by that same instinct, usually also investing in closing off these other, unrelated classes of attack at the same time.
14. Why the Entire Web Pushed Toward HTTPS
blocks.text: 14. Why the Entire Web Pushed Toward HTTPS

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273537147-459842326.png
blocks.alt: Search engines treat HTTPS as a genuine, if modest, ranking signal, all else being equal

blocks.content: Beyond the direct security benefit, major search engines explicitly treat HTTPS as a ranking signal, an otherwise identical page served over HTTPS can rank slightly higher than the same page served over plain HTTP. Combined with browsers actively flagging plain HTTP sites as Not Secure in the address bar itself, these two pressures together are why the overwhelming majority of the web now defaults to HTTPS everywhere, not just on pages that handle logins or payments.

Free, automated certificate authorities removed the last real excuse for staying on plain HTTP, obtaining and renewing a valid certificate no longer costs money or requires manual, error prone paperwork the way it once did, turning HTTPS from a costly extra step into something closer to a default configuration choice.

The example below implements exactly the chain of trust described earlier: given a certificate chain from a website up through an intermediate authority to a root, it verifies each certificate's issuer genuinely matches the next certificate's own subject, and that the final root is actually in the trusted set, the same check a real browser performs before ever showing a page as secure.
Worked Example

A developer notices their own site's HTTPS padlock occasionally shows a warning icon instead of the usual secure lock. Investigating, they find the page's own HTML correctly loads every script and stylesheet over HTTPS, but one third party analytics widget is still hardcoded to load its tracking script over plain HTTP from years ago, before that vendor supported HTTPS at all.

That single mixed content resource is exactly what triggers the warning, even though every first party asset on the page is genuinely secure. Updating the one hardcoded URL to HTTPS resolves the warning entirely, without touching anything else on the page.

The broader lesson generalizes well beyond this one analytics widget, any third party dependency, an embedded widget, an old CDN link, an advertising script, carries the exact same risk if it was ever configured before that vendor supported HTTPS, which is why a genuine security review checks every external resource a page loads, not only the page's own first party code.
Common Mistakes

["Assuming HTTPS alone guarantees a site is trustworthy, when it only guarantees the connection itself is encrypted and the domain ownership is verified","Loading even one script, image, or stylesheet over plain HTTP on an otherwise HTTPS page, quietly reintroducing mixed content risk","Letting a certificate's renewal depend on someone remembering a calendar date instead of automating it well ahead of expiry","Treating HTTP/2's multiplexing and HTTP/3's move to UDP as unrelated performance tweaks, rather than each one solving a specific, named bottleneck the previous version genuinely had"]
items: Assuming HTTPS alone guarantees a site is trustworthy, when it only guarantees the connection itself is encrypted and the domain ownership is verified
Loading even one script, image, or stylesheet over plain HTTP on an otherwise HTTPS page, quietly reintroducing mixed content risk
Letting a certificate's renewal depend on someone remembering a calendar date instead of automating it well ahead of expiry
Treating HTTP/2's multiplexing and HTTP/3's move to UDP as unrelated performance tweaks, rather than each one solving a specific, named bottleneck the previous version genuinely had

blocks.content: Practice

Open the browser developer tools on any HTTPS website you use daily, inspect its certificate details, and identify the domain name, the issuing Certificate Authority, and the expiry date. Then check the network tab for any request that was made over plain HTTP instead of HTTPS, and explain what risk, if any, that specific request actually introduces.

As a second exercise, look up whether that same site sends an HSTS header in its response, and if so, note the duration it specifies, then explain in your own words what would happen if you typed the plain http version of that same domain directly into your address bar.
Key Takeaway

HTTP and HTTPS share the exact same request and response structure, methods, headers, status codes, the entire difference is that HTTPS wraps that traffic in TLS, providing encryption, authentication through a certificate chain of trust, and integrity checking that plain HTTP has none of. A valid certificate proves a server owns its domain, never that the organization behind it deserves your trust, and real production systems have to treat certificate renewal and mixed content as things to actively guard against, not problems that simply take care of themselves.
